extracted.intended_audience: fiction and nonfiction writers (indie and trad) who want practical guidance on using beta readers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on who to recruit as beta readers, when to use them during the drafting/revision cycle, what to ask them, and how to interpret and act on their feedback. Focused on authors preparing fiction or nonfiction manuscripts for revision or publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers-only beta selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer non-writers (readers) because they’re more authentic, representative, and jargon-free — ideally from your target audience, familiar with and liking your genre, with a sharp mind and attention to detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose non-friends when possible to avoid softened responses. Consider specialty readers (legal, historical, mental health) or sensitivity readers when material is outside your experience. Use readers later in the process (see timing) when the manuscript is polished enough for a non-writer to read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers-only beta selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer fellow writers because they can spot and articulate plot, pacing, and character issues and explain craft problems in more specific terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware writers may revert to how they would have written it (temptation to rewrite). Use writer-betas for early drafts, when stuck, or when you need craft-level diagnosis, but guard against receiving feedback that simply remakes the work in another writer’s voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a mix of writers and readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Many authors use a variety of beta readers—writers and non-writers—to get complementary perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix can include family, trusted critique partners, target-audience representatives, strangers, and ‘intelligent friends.’ One respondent’s practical mix: one-third supporters/cheerleaders, one-third tough critics, one-third unpredictable ‘wild cards.’ A variety gives fuller understanding of strengths and weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage-appropriate beta deployment (when to use whom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different kinds of beta readers are useful at different points: early draft, revision stage, and final/polished manuscript (these aren’t rigid but imply different uses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fellow writers are most helpful for early drafts and ongoing critique or when you’re stuck; non-writers are better later as a test audience/quality-assurance once the manuscript is as polished as you can make it. Avoid showing non-writers material that still requires heavy structural work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and communicate what you want from betas
rubrics_metrics.description: Know—and tell—what you want from a beta reader; expectations may differ by stage and reader type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a list of specific questions about structure, clarity, continuity, and character development to focus comments (otherwise risk vague praise or line-edit impulses). Alternatively, if you want raw reactions, leave feedback open-ended; weigh trade-offs between priming readers and getting authentic responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed questions vs open-ended feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking specific questions focuses comments on issues you care about; leaving feedback open-ended lets readers report what they actually felt and notice things you didn’t prime them to see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need actionable input on particular problems, give targeted prompts. If you want unfiltered reader reaction (what stands out, what confuses), ask for open responses. Consider combining both approaches for different readers/stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek diversity of background and viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Select beta readers with varied backgrounds and perspectives depending on your goals—heterogeneous groups for broad testing or specific readers for targeted feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include at least some representatives of your target audience and sometimes at least one reader outside your genre to test broader appeal. Choose specialty or sensitivity readers when the book involves expertise or lived experiences outside your own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the number of beta readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Too many beta readers can create conflicting advice and dilute the author’s intent; respondents typically used between two and twelve betas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ‘ten people’s worth of changes’ that can change the book into something else. If many betas disagree, that creates another decision problem—focus on commonalities and your own vision rather than implementing every suggestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vet for quality and match expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Beta reader quality varies widely; usefulness depends on who you find and whether they match your expectations for feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for readers who understand your goals and will provide the kind of input you need. Willingness to give feedback doesn’t equal ability to give useful, actionable feedback. Consider asking for examples of past beta work, or starting with a shorter sample, to gauge fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect limited craft-specific, actionable fixes from betas
rubrics_metrics.description: Unpaid/non-professional betas often report reactions but may not give craft-specific, actionable advice on how to fix problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may need to “reverse engineer” reader reactions into specific craft fixes, or follow up with writer-betas or paid editors for deeper craft work. Use beta feedback as signal, not a prescriptive plan of edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight feedback by consensus and resonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Give more weight to problems multiple readers point out—especially if identified by both writer and non-writer betas—or feedback that strongly resonates with you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If several readers independently cite the same weakness, that’s a reliable signal to address it. Individual outlier comments should be considered but not necessarily adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate roles: beta readers vs critique partners vs editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Beta readers act as proxies for general readers; critique partners are peer writers who may swap work and provide craft-level feedback; editors are professionals who make a manuscript marketable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use critique partners for iterative craft work, beta readers for broader reader-response testing, and paid editors when you need substantive developmental or line editing you can’t get from betas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specialty and sensitivity readers when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When your book involves specialized knowledge or experiences outside your own, recruit expert or sensitivity readers to spot factual, cultural, or experiential inaccuracies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialty readers can check legal, historical, medical, or other details. Sensitivity readers can flag cultural or identity-related problems. These roles are different from general betas and should be recruited specifically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formats and tools for sharing manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Common formats include PDF, Word (with Track Changes), Google Docs (collaborative comments), hardcopy for table reads, and audio recordings for flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PDFs and Word docs are widely used; Track Changes allows inline corrections; Google Docs allows shared visibility of comments which can be useful in group settings (less private). Consider a table read or having someone read aloud to hear flow. Choose the format that best suits the reader’s habits and the kind of feedback you want.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask readers to record questions they had while reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Request that beta readers write down every question they had about the story so you can address those holes within the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical tactic: have betas note questions so you can answer them directly in the text (e.g., clarify dropped threads, explain confusing transitions). This produces actionable targets for revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware friendship and social pressures that soften feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Friends and acquaintances may give gentler, less useful feedback (the ‘yes me to death’ problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want blunt, honest responses, recruit readers without a vested interest or explicitly request candidness. Set expectations up front about the level of honesty you need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use beta readers to validate overall story and restore confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond pointing out problems, beta readers can reassure you that the story as a whole works and restore confidence after long writing periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include at least some readers who will read for enjoyment/story rather than edit, so you can confirm whether the ‘forest’ is intact even if some ‘trees’ need pruning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for logistical limitations (time, commitment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beta readers may lack the time or interest to finish an entire manuscript even if they agree to read it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set clear timelines and expectations up front. Consider offering format options (PDF, Kindle, hardcopy) and check in on progress. If a beta drops out midstream, decide whether to count their partial feedback or recruit a replacement.
